title: the mountain ahead
hookLine: the mountain ahead; "mind is the forerunner"

cards: Three weeks. Look at your strand. Karma, the three jewels, sati, the four noble truths, dana, Vesak, rebirth.
Dukkha, tanha, nirvana, the eightfold path. The precepts, anicca, anatta. Metta, karuna, the sangha, the Jataka, equanimity, the middle way.

Twenty words, the everyday vocabulary of a Buddhist life. Those are the foothills. Tomorrow the path starts climbing: the Buddha's whole life, told like a serial, from a queen's dream to his last words.
So today, from the top of the foothills, a look up at the mountain. One small book of verses, and its very first line.

teach.b: The Dhammapada. Four hundred and twenty-three short verses, in twenty-six chapters, kept in the Pali canon and remembered as the Buddha's own sayings.
Its verses are chanted, memorized and preached on in Buddhist communities to this day. The name has two halves.
Dhamma, the teaching, the way things are. And pada, which means a foot, a step, a path, and also a line of verse. So it's the path of the teaching, or the verses of the teaching, and both are right.

Every step is a line. You've already heard it several times in these three weeks: the fragrance that travels against the wind, nirvana as the highest happiness, hatred ceasing by love, the rock in the wind.
Now here's where it starts. The very first verse.
Modern translators render it something like: mind is the forerunner of all things.
An old English translation reads: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts." Then, across the first two verses, two images.
If someone speaks or acts from a harmful mind, pain follows, like the wheel of a cart following the ox's foot.
And if someone speaks or acts from a clear, good mind, happiness follows them, "like a shadow that never leaves him."
Notice what the first verse is doing. It isn't telling you what to believe about the universe. It's pointing you back at your own mind, the one place you can actually start.
The whole path so far, from day one's intention to the noticing and the metta, begins right there.

how: Buddhists, especially in Theravada countries, memorize and chant verses of the Dhammapada, hear them explained in sermons with the stories that go with each verse, and keep a copy at home as a small book of daily wisdom.

games.q: what's inside the book — tap the pairs.
p: a step, a path, a line of verse

s: the Dhammapada is a long book of stories
it's 423 short verses in 26 chapters. the stories come in later commentaries.
pada can mean both a step and a line of verse
so the title is the path of the teaching, or the verses of the teaching.
its first verse is about the mind
mind is the forerunner: "all that we are is the result of what we have thought."

games.q: the first verse gives two pictures. someone acts from a harmful mind. what follows them?
o: pain, like a wheel following the ox's foot.
games.why: pain follows, like the cart wheel behind the ox. the second verse flips it: from a good mind, happiness follows, like a shadow.

practice: The bell gives you about seventy-five seconds. Think back over these three weeks.

Let the words drift past: the seed of an intention, three bows, the gatekeeper, the wobble in the wheel, the open hand, the passing leaf, the monkey on the branch. Don't try to remember them all. Just notice which one has stuck.
Which came back to you on an ordinary day, without being asked? Hold that one word. Breathe with it.

wordCard.voice: The Dhammapada. The path of the teaching, verses of the teaching: four hundred and twenty-three verses that start with the mind. Twenty-first word, and camp one is done.

carryVoice: Your line: what you think, you become. Tomorrow the story begins, with a queen's dream of a white elephant. Day twenty-one.
